finding: The live range of $380-$1,475 is about right, and it is wide because it spans two different jobs: an external pump driven by the accessory belt, and a pump buried behind the timing belt. Built totals (pump + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Corolla about $251-$458 (1.6-2.0 hr); midsize 2016 Camry about $242-$487 (1.4-2.0 hr); truck 2016 F-150 5.0L about $171-$518 (1.0-2.0 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i (electric pump) about $569-$944 (1.0-2.0 hr). The low ends fall under the live floor of $380, but that is not evidence the floor is too high: they price the pump alone at online prices ($51-$74) with no coolant, thermostat or belt, and they use manufacturer warranty times, which are the least a shop bills. Every outside estimate starts at $353 or more, and RepairPal's parts figure alone is $525-$598. How solid the labor times are: none is a manufacturer time for the exact example vehicle. The economy low end is GM's 1.6 hr for a 2011-2014 Cruze 1.4L (1.3 hr plus 0.3 hr to fill the cooling system); the midsize low end is Honda's 1.4 hr for a 2013-2016 Accord 4-cylinder (the same bulletin gives 1.7-1.8 hr for the CR-V); the truck low end is a parts seller's 1-hour estimate for the earlier 2011-2014 F-150 5.0L; the luxury figure is a parts seller's 'hour or two' do-it-yourself estimate for the same engine. The high end for the three belt-driven classes is one general statement ('one or two hours') from a how-to guide, not a book time; outside estimators assume 2-4 hours, so real quotes will often run above our totals. Top of the range: none of the four examples has a pump driven by the timing belt. As a sourced check on that kind of job, Honda's recall bulletin 19-045 allows 3.1-3.4 hr to inspect and replace the timing belt on the 3.5L V6 (2019 Odyssey 3.1, 2018-2019 Pilot 3.2, 2019 Ridgeline 3.4); the pump sits behind that belt, the bulletin does not include changing it, and the allowance covers no coolant drain and refill, so the true pump job is longer. An Aisin TKH-002 timing belt kit with water pump for the Pilot and Odyssey was $282.99 (one retailer only; list $448.42). That builds to roughly $655-$827 as a floor for a timing-belt-and-pump job with aftermarket parts, comfortably inside the live ceiling; with dealer parts, a longer real-world labor time and a higher labor rate the $1,475 top is plausible, but we could not build a total that high from stated figures, so the ceiling is supported by the outside estimates (which cite 4-8 hours for these engines) rather than proven.
extras: A quote often adds coolant and a cooling system bleed or pressure test, a thermostat, a drive belt, new pump bolts or gaskets, a diagnosis fee, shop supplies, coolant disposal, and sales tax. On engines where the timing belt drives the pump, shops normally quote the timing belt, tensioner and idlers in the same job, which raises the total a lot. The parts figures here are the pump (with its gasket where included) only. Sourced example of that bigger job: on Honda's 3.5L V6 the maker's own warranty allowance just to replace the timing belt is 3.1-3.4 hours (recall bulletin 19-045), and an aftermarket timing belt kit that includes the water pump was $282.99 at one retailer (Aisin TKH-002, Pilot and Odyssey).
